title: 5 Classroom Management Tips For Every Teacher
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin presents five foundational but frequently overlooked classroom management tips he considers the backbone of exceptional teaching: teaching highly detailed routines for every repeatable moment, making an unwavering commitment to a classroom management plan, building behavior-influencing rapport through simple pleasantness, spending more time observing than micromanaging, and taking full personal responsibility for students' learning and behavior rather than blaming outside circumstances. He frames summer as the ideal moment for teachers to take inventory of the prior year and commit to these principles going forward. The piece closes with an encouraging call to take the first step toward implementing these practices, framing the effort as scary but achievable and worthwhile.
points: Teach highly detailed, step-by-step routines for every repeatable classroom moment starting on day one.
Commit unwaveringly to the classroom management plan—inconsistency erodes trust and pushes teachers toward yelling, scolding, or sarcasm.
Build behavior-influencing rapport simply by being consistently pleasant, open to laughter, and free of friction with students.
Spend more time observing from a distance and less time micromanaging, which breeds needy, dependent students.
Take full responsibility for students' learning and behavior instead of blaming outside circumstances like parents or environment.
quotes: Well-taught routines, performed with excellence, are among the clearest indicators of exceptional teaching.
An inconsistently followed classroom management plan is one of the most common teacher mistakes. It’s also among the most detrimental.
If you're merely pleasant in your interactions with students, if you're open to laughter and seeing the humor in your classroom... then behavior-influencing rapport will grow naturally.
Most teachers talk too much, help too much, and are seen too much. The truth is, micromanagement breeds needy, demanding, and dependent students.
But in the end, blaming parents, video games, or the neighborhood they live in, for example, solves nothing and makes creating the classroom you really want an impossibility.
It’s scary to step out into the unknown. It’s scary to dare yourself to be more than just another teacher.
